newsitem.title: MEXICO: Leftist faces uphill task at helm of Mexico City.
newsitem.headline: Leftist faces uphill task at helm of Mexico City.

text.p: Victorious leftist Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, the first elected mayor of modern Mexico City, faces an uphill struggle to succeed in governing a huge capital racked by poverty, pollution and crime.

The candidate of the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) swept to a historic win in Sunday's voting, well over 20 percentage points ahead of his nearest rival. But now he has to put the euphoria of victory behind him and concentrate on the challenge ahead.

"If he thinks the hardest hurdle will have been jumped on July 6, then he is wrong. If he and his team jump on the triumphalistic wave without understanding the undercurrent that is coming, then they are wrong," political analyst Denise Dresser wrote.

Cardenas' task is monumental. He will directly govern the Federal District, an enclave of central areas of the city with 8.5 million people and the offices of the federal government. He will also have to face the pressures of a metropolitan area of 17 million people, half of whom flood into the capital's heart to work but who are ruled by a governor from the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).
Crime has soared since the 1994 peso devaluation, which forced hundreds of thousands out of work. Bank robberies are commonplace and murders and kidnappings are multiplying.
"Mexico City is a bit like Velcro: Everything that is bad can stick to you," Delal Baer, a political scientist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, said.

The devaluation brought soaring inflation, slashed real incomes and forced many jobless city residents to resort to begging or washing windshields to survive. Pollution is so bad some Western embassies in the city allow only short terms in Mexico. Diplomats with families are often advised not to apply for Mexican posts because of lead and ozone levels in the air.
Cardenas on Monday appeared aware of his tasks. "It is a great challenge to live up to the hopes of the people that gave the PRD its victory," he told radio station Formula 21.

But the 63-year-old son of former President Lazaro Cardenas will have his work cut out to make good on campaign pledges to clamp down on corruption in the police force, tackle pollution and cut crime. Those promises have been made in the past, and the problems remain.
Political careers have also withered in his post, which, partly because of its sensitivity, was previously filled by a mayor appointed by Mexico's president.

One problem for Cardenas, analysts said, is that he has only three years after taking office on Dec. 5 to prove his worth. If he overcomes the odds and shines in power, he is tipped to be the PRD candidate for the presidency in 2000.
Cardenas said on Monday the city needed a transition team before he took office for a peaceful handover of power and discussion of next year's city budget.
"It has to be a peaceful and constructive handover ... and we have to look how we are going to participate in the preparation of the 1998 budget," he told TV network Televisa.
Wrangling over next year's budget is expected to start well ahead of his official takeover. Nor is it certain how well he will work with President Ernesto Zedillo of the PRI.
Mexico's president retains key powers in the capital including the right to name its chief of police and chief prosecutor. And the mayor cannot borrow money without his permission.
Analysts believe Zedillo and Cardenas will have to enter into a cohabitation deal to avoid the sullying of both in the political battles that probably lie ahead.

"The distance between the president and the mayor will be healthy but difficult. ... The biggest challenge for the so-called Tony Blair of the Mexican left is the enormous flood of expectations that will be faced by his administration," Dresser wrote in the Reforma daily. Blair was elected Britain's Labor Party prime minister in May after 18 years of Conservative rule.
